Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BEIJING, China (CNN) -- For years, doctors and patients have been using DNA analysis to diagnose anything from paternity to predisposition to inherited disease. Now, Chinese scientists say genetic testing can identify inherent "talents" as well. The results can reveal athletic or musical talents but cannot necessarily identify the next Yao Ming. By examining the DNA from a simple cheek swab, scientists at Shanghai Biochip Co., one of China's largest biotechnology companies, say they can uncover a person's natural strengths and weaknesses with 99 percent accuracy. They test eleven genes that they say correspond to memory, swiftness, thinking, comprehension, emotion, adventure, braveness, focus ability, perseverance, vigor and physical strength. According to the company, specific combinations of the genes can reveal whether someone is genetically predisposed to being highly intelligent, athletic, musical and more. In the case of memory, the scientists examine the gene known as BDNF, the Brain Derived Neurotrophic Factor gene. Research by America's National Institute of Health suggests that different variants of the BDNF gene correspond to different competences in episodic memory (the ability to recall recent events) as well as different activity-levels in the hippocampus (the area of the brain that mediates memory).  See photos of the children's summer camp in China where such testing occurs » . Each person has one of three possible BDNF variants: AA, AG and GG. Each variant or base pair refers to the two gene components that make up each gene on the DNA's double helix. Most people have the GG variant, which indicates "normal" memory. Fewer people have the AG base pair, which corresponds to "above average" memory. AA is the rarest and strongest type of memory gene variant. "The AA genotype is the best in memory. (Someone with an AA pairing) will learn something easy and remember the result longer than others can," said Yang Yanqing, the lab's technical director. Once lab technicians determine the base pairs for each of the eleven talent genes, specialists draw conclusions about a person's broader characteristics and even make career recommendations based a person's talent level in each of the eleven categories. "This child is very thoughtful and focused," Shanghai Biochip's Healthcare Director Huang Xinhua explained while looking over a girl's test results. "I suggest she go into management." Although the results can also reveal athletic or musical talents, genetic testing will not necessarily be able to identify the next Yao Ming or Yo-Yo Ma. DNA analysis only provides an indication of someone's talent potential, not their realized skill-level, the scientists say. "It's not like genes decide everything. Genes just decide 30 to 60 percent. The rest is post-natal. A child's upbringing, nutrition, and education are all very much related," said Huang. Still for many Chinese parents, it is worth knowing that extra 30 to 60 percent more about their child. The lab, which conducts many other types of DNA tests, has seen a surge in the demand for genetic talent tests, most of the requests come from parents on behalf of their children. In a country where, by law, most couples can only have one child, parents seem to be turning to biotechnology to ensure their only child reaches his or her full potential.

BEIJING, China (CNN) — DNA testing has long been used by physicians and patients for purposes ranging from establishing paternity to assessing the risk of inherited illnesses. Chinese researchers now say the same kind of genetic analysis may also point to a person’s natural “talents.”

According to scientists, the findings may suggest abilities in areas such as sports or music, though they cannot reliably single out a future Yao Ming. Researchers at Shanghai Biochip Co., one of China’s biggest biotechnology firms, say that by analyzing DNA collected with a simple cheek swab, they can determine an individual’s inborn strengths and weaknesses with 99 percent accuracy.

The company examines 11 genes that it says are linked to memory, speed, reasoning, understanding, emotion, adventurousness, courage, concentration, persistence, vitality and physical strength. It says certain gene combinations can indicate whether a person has a genetic tendency toward high intelligence, athletic ability, musical skill and other traits.

For memory, the scientists focus on a gene called BDNF, or Brain Derived Neurotrophic Factor. Research from the U.S. National Institutes of Health indicates that different forms of the BDNF gene are associated with varying abilities in episodic memory — the capacity to remember recent events — as well as different levels of activity in the hippocampus, the part of the brain involved in memory.

Each person carries one of three possible BDNF variants: AA, AG or GG. These variants, or base-pair combinations, refer to the two genetic components that form each gene along DNA’s double helix. The GG type is the most common and is said to represent “normal” memory. The AG pairing is less common and is associated with “above average” memory. The AA variant is the rarest and is considered the strongest memory-related form.

“The AA genotype is the best in memory. (Someone with an AA pairing) will learn something easy and remember the result longer than others can,” said Yang Yanqing, the laboratory’s technical director.

After technicians identify the base-pair types for all 11 so-called talent genes, specialists interpret the results to describe a person’s overall traits and may even suggest career paths based on that person’s scores in the 11 categories.

“This child is very thoughtful and focused,” said Huang Xinhua, Shanghai Biochip’s healthcare director, as she reviewed a girl’s results. “I suggest she go into management.”

The company says the tests may also indicate potential in athletics or music, but they will not necessarily discover the next Yao Ming or Yo-Yo Ma. The researchers emphasize that DNA analysis can only suggest a person’s possible talent, not measure the level of ability they will ultimately develop.

“It’s not like genes decide everything. Genes just decide 30 to 60 percent. The rest is post-natal. A child’s upbringing, nutrition, and education are all very much related,” Huang said.

Even so, many Chinese parents appear eager to learn that additional 30 to 60 percent about their children. The laboratory, which performs a variety of DNA tests, has reported a sharp increase in demand for genetic talent testing, with most requests coming from parents seeking information about their children.

In China, where most couples are legally limited to having one child, parents appear to be looking to biotechnology as a way to help their only child develop as fully as possible.

counterfactuals.output:
**Chinese biotech company draws scrutiny for DNA tests it says can identify children’s “inherited talents”**

*By [Reporter Name]*

A Chinese biotechnology company is marketing DNA cheek-swab tests to parents who hope to learn whether their children may have genetic advantages in areas such as memory, athletic ability, musical aptitude, focus and intelligence — claims that have sparked interest among families and concern among scientists.

The company says its test analyzes genetic markers associated with traits linked to learning, physical performance and cognitive development. Parents collect a saliva or cheek-swab sample from a child and send it to a laboratory, where the DNA is screened. A report is then returned outlining what the company describes as the child’s “potential” strengths and weaknesses.

Promotional materials reviewed by media outlets suggest the test is aimed at helping parents make early decisions about education, extracurricular activities and training. Some packages reportedly include recommendations on whether a child may be suited to sports, music lessons, academic enrichment or other specialized programs.

But geneticists and child-development experts warn that such claims may go far beyond what science can currently support.

While researchers have identified genetic variants that can be statistically associated with certain traits, experts say complex abilities like intelligence, musical talent, attention and athletic performance are influenced by thousands of genes interacting with environment, education, nutrition, family support, coaching and chance.

“No DNA test can reliably tell you whether a child will become a great pianist, a top athlete or a gifted student,” said one researcher familiar with behavioral genetics. “At best, these tests may point to very small probabilities. They should not be used to define a child’s future.”

The rise of talent-focused genetic testing comes as consumer DNA services expand across China and other parts of Asia. Once primarily used for ancestry, health risk screening or paternity testing, some companies are now positioning genetic analysis as a tool for parenting and education.

Critics say that raises ethical questions. They worry that parents may pressure children into activities based on a genetic report, overlook interests that do not match the results, or label children as having limited potential in certain areas. There are also concerns about the privacy and long-term storage of minors’ genetic data.

Children cannot meaningfully consent to having their genetic information analyzed and stored, bioethicists say. DNA data can reveal sensitive information not only about the child, but also about relatives.

Regulators in several countries have cautioned against overinterpreting direct-to-consumer genetic tests, particularly when they involve children or make predictions about behavioral traits. In China, authorities have tightened oversight of genetic testing in some medical contexts, but the consumer market remains a fast-moving space.

The company maintains that its test is not meant to determine a child’s destiny, but rather to provide parents with additional information. It says genetics is only one factor and that upbringing and environment remain important.

Scientists agree on that point — but say the danger lies in how the results are marketed and understood.

“Parents want to give their children every advantage,” said a child psychologist. “But reducing a child’s abilities to a DNA report can be misleading. Curiosity, motivation, practice and emotional support matter enormously.”

For now, experts advise parents to treat talent DNA tests with caution. A cheek swab may reveal biological clues, they say, but it cannot replace watching what a child enjoys, how they learn and where they choose to grow.

counterfactuals.output:
# Genetic “Talent Testing” in China: Promise, Pressure, and the Limits of DNA

In recent years, a niche industry has emerged in China offering parents genetic tests that claim to reveal a child’s hidden talents. Marketed as tools for educational planning, these services often promise insights into traits such as musical ability, athletic potential, memory, creativity, emotional resilience, or even leadership. A cheek swab or saliva sample is sent to a laboratory, and parents receive a report linking variations in certain genes to possible strengths and weaknesses.

The appeal is easy to understand. In a highly competitive education system, many parents are eager for any information that might help them choose the “right” path for their child—piano or painting, mathematics or language, sprinting or swimming. But scientists remain deeply skeptical of claims that a genetic test can reliably predict future talent or success.

## A Market Built on Parental Anxiety

China’s interest in talent testing cannot be separated from broader social pressures. For decades, the one-child policy meant that many families had only one child on whom to focus their hopes, resources, and expectations. The phrase “little emperor” was sometimes used to describe the intense attention given to only children, but the reality was often more serious: parents and grandparents invested heavily in tutoring, extracurricular lessons, and elite schooling.

In this environment, genetic testing companies found a receptive audience. If a DNA test could supposedly suggest whether a child had an advantage in sports, music, memory, or concentration, it could be marketed as a scientific shortcut for parents trying to make difficult choices.

Some companies have advertised tests for “innate talent” or “children’s potential,” offering reports that rank traits such as intelligence, curiosity, stress tolerance, endurance, and artistic ability. The language often blends scientific terminology with educational ambition, creating an impression that a child’s future can be mapped from their genome.

## Genes Commonly Used in Talent Claims

Many genetic talent tests cite real genes that have been studied in relation to brain function, physical performance, or behavior. However, the existence of a scientific study does not mean a gene can be used to predict a child’s destiny.

One commonly mentioned gene is **BDNF**, which stands for brain-derived neurotrophic factor. BDNF plays an important role in brain development, learning, memory, and neural plasticity—the brain’s ability to adapt and form new connections. A well-known variation in this gene, often called **Val66Met**, has been studied for possible links to memory performance, anxiety, and response to training or stress.

Because BDNF is involved in learning and the brain, it is tempting for testing companies to connect it with academic or artistic potential. But the relationship is not straightforward. A BDNF variant may have small statistical associations with certain traits in some populations, but it cannot determine whether a child will become a gifted musician, a top student, or a creative thinker.

Other genes sometimes used in commercial testing include:

- **ACTN3**, often associated with muscle performance. One variant is more common among elite sprint and power athletes, while another is more common in endurance contexts. Still, training, coaching, nutrition, motivation, and opportunity matter enormously.
- **COMT**, involved in dopamine metabolism and sometimes discussed in relation to attention, stress response, or cognitive performance. Its effects are complex and context-dependent.
- **DRD2** and **DRD4**, dopamine receptor genes sometimes linked in studies to novelty-seeking, motivation, or attention-related traits, though findings are often inconsistent.
- **5-HTTLPR**, a serotonin-related genetic variant studied in relation to emotion and stress sensitivity, but controversial because results have not always replicated.

These genes are biologically meaningful, but most human traits are influenced by thousands of genetic variants, each contributing a very small effect. Talent is not controlled by a single gene, or even by a small panel of genes.

## The Science: Real Genetics, Weak Predictions

Modern genetics has shown that traits such as height, disease risk, and some aspects of cognition can have heritable components. But heritability is often misunderstood. Saying a trait is “heritable” does not mean it is fixed, inevitable, or easily predictable for an individual child.

Complex abilities—such as musical talent, mathematical skill, athletic excellence, or leadership—are shaped by many interacting factors:

- genetics  
- family environment  
- education quality  
- practice and training  
- nutrition and health  
- emotional support  
- socioeconomic opportunity  
- motivation and personality  
- cultural expectations  
- chance events and mentorship  

Even in areas where genetics plays a role, DNA usually provides probabilities, not certainties. A child with a genetic variant associated with muscle power will not become an elite athlete without years of training. A child without that variant may still excel through discipline, coaching, and passion.

This is why many geneticists and educators criticize talent testing as scientifically premature. The tests may use genuine genetic markers, but the interpretation often goes far beyond what the evidence supports.

## Why Parents Still Buy the Tests

Despite skepticism, demand persists because the tests promise clarity in a world of uncertainty. Chinese parents, like parents everywhere, want to make good decisions for their children. Should they invest in violin lessons? Should the child focus on swimming? Is the child naturally suited for science? Could the test reveal a hidden advantage?

For families under intense educational pressure, even a questionable tool may feel useful. A colorful report with scientific language can seem more objective than guesswork. Some parents may not believe the test completely but use it as one more piece of information.

There is also a cultural and economic dimension. As China’s middle class has expanded, parents have spent more on private education, enrichment programs, and health-related services. Genetic talent testing fits into a broader market of child development products promising optimization and competitive advantage.

## Ethical Concerns

The rise of genetic talent testing raises several ethical questions.

First, there is the risk of labeling children too early. If a report suggests that a child has low musical potential or weak athletic ability, parents may discourage activities the child enjoys. Conversely, if a report suggests “high potential,” a child may be pushed into training they do not want.

Second, genetic data is sensitive. DNA contains information not only about the child but also about biological relatives. Parents may not fully understand how the data will be stored, shared, or used in the future.

Third, these tests can reinforce social inequality. Wealthier families can afford more testing, tutoring, and specialized training, while poorer families may not. If genetic reports are treated as authoritative, they could add another layer of pressure and stratification to education.

Finally, there is the danger of genetic determinism—the belief that genes decide a person’s fate. This view is not supported by modern science. Genes influence development, but they do not write a complete script for life.

## Skepticism from Scientists and Educators

Many experts argue that current talent tests oversell what genetics can do. While genetic research has advanced rapidly, predicting individual talent remains extremely difficult. Most studies identify small associations across large groups, not precise forecasts for one child.

A genetic variant may slightly increase the probability of a trait under certain conditions, but it does not guarantee an outcome. Moreover, many studies were conducted in specific populations and may not apply universally. Results can vary by ethnicity, environment, sample size, and research design.

Educators also warn that focusing too much on innate ability can undermine effort. Children who are told they are “naturally gifted” may fear failure, while those told they lack talent may stop trying. Research on learning often emphasizes the importance of persistence, curiosity, feedback, and a growth mindset.

## A More Responsible Use of Genetics

Genetic information can be valuable in medicine, especially for diagnosing inherited disorders, identifying disease risks, or guiding certain treatments. But using DNA to predict talent is far less reliable.

A responsible approach would treat genetic results, if used at all, as limited and uncertain—not as instructions for a child’s future. Parents should be cautious of any company claiming that a DNA test can identify a child’s best career, sport, or artistic path.

Rather than asking, “What does my child’s DNA say they should become?” a better question may be: “What does my child enjoy, and how can I support their development?”

## Conclusion

Genetic talent testing in China reflects a powerful mix of scientific curiosity, commercial opportunity, and parental pressure. Genes such as BDNF, ACTN3, and COMT are genuinely involved in brain function, physical performance, or behavior, but their effects are limited and complex. They cannot determine whether a child will become a brilliant pianist, a champion athlete, or a successful entrepreneur.

The popularity of these tests reveals less about the certainty of genetics than about the uncertainty faced by parents. In a society shaped by fierce educational competition and the legacy of the one-child policy, the promise of early answers can be very attractive.

But talent is not a barcode hidden in DNA. It develops through practice, support, opportunity, health, motivation, and time. Genes may influence the starting point, but they do not decide the finish line.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

Chinese researchers are exploring whether DNA analysis can be used to assess a person’s natural potential in areas such as memory, physical strength, perseverance and even risk-taking behavior — a field that blends genetics, psychology and sports science, while raising major questions about how far such predictions can reliably go.

The idea rests on a simple premise: human traits are influenced, in part, by genes. By scanning certain genetic markers, scientists say they may be able to estimate whether someone has biological tendencies that could support particular abilities — for example, endurance, explosive power, stress tolerance or aspects of cognitive performance.

But researchers and ethicists emphasize that DNA is not destiny. Education, family background, nutrition, training, sleep, social support, motivation, trauma and opportunity can all shape a person’s development. Even if a genetic profile suggests an advantage in one area, that potential may never emerge without the right environment. Conversely, people without a favorable genetic profile can still excel through practice and discipline.

## What scientists say DNA may reveal

Chinese scientists working in genomics and talent assessment have pointed to research linking specific genes or gene regions to measurable physical and psychological traits.

In sports science, some gene variants have long been studied for their possible connection to athletic performance. For instance, the **ACTN3** gene is often associated with fast-twitch muscle fibers, which are important for sprinting and explosive strength. Another gene, **ACE**, has been studied in relation to endurance and cardiovascular performance. While neither gene can predict whether a person will become an elite athlete, researchers say such markers may offer clues about physical predispositions.

For cognitive traits, scientists have examined genes involved in brain development, neurotransmitter signaling and synaptic plasticity — the brain’s ability to form and reorganize connections. These biological processes are related to learning and memory, though the genetics of intelligence and memory are far more complex than a single gene.

Traits such as bravery, perseverance and resilience are even more difficult to define. Scientists may look at genes connected to dopamine, serotonin, adrenaline and stress-response systems, which can influence emotional regulation, novelty-seeking, fear response and persistence under pressure. However, such behaviors are strongly shaped by upbringing, culture and personal experience.

## A tool for guidance, not a crystal ball

Advocates of genetic analysis say the technology could one day help parents, teachers or coaches better understand a child’s strengths and developmental needs. In theory, a child with markers linked to endurance might be encouraged toward long-distance sports, while another with traits associated with quick reaction speed and power might be guided toward sprinting or martial arts.

Some researchers argue that genetic testing could make training more personalized. Athletes, for example, might use DNA information to adjust exercise intensity, recovery time or injury-prevention strategies. In education, genetic insights could potentially be combined with behavioral assessments to support learning strategies.

But many experts warn against overstating the science. Most human talents are **polygenic**, meaning they are influenced by hundreds or thousands of genetic variants, each with a tiny effect. They are also deeply affected by environment. A DNA test might identify probabilities, not certainties.

A person’s memory, for example, depends not only on inherited biology but also on schooling, attention, mental health, sleep quality, language exposure and practice. Physical strength depends on training, diet, hormones, injury history and access to facilities. Perseverance can be cultivated through parenting, education, mentorship and life experience.

## Environmental factors still matter

Scientists involved in the field acknowledge that genetic analysis cannot replace hard work or supportive conditions. Even the most promising biological predisposition may be limited by poor nutrition, inadequate training, chronic stress or lack of opportunity.

Likewise, environmental support can help overcome genetic disadvantages. A child who is not naturally strong can build strength through training. A student who struggles with memory can improve through study techniques, repetition and proper sleep. A person who is fearful in childhood may develop courage through experience, confidence and social support.

This “gene-environment interaction” is central to modern genetics. Genes may influence how a person responds to the environment, but the environment also influences how genetic potential is expressed. In some cases, lifestyle can affect gene activity through epigenetic mechanisms — chemical changes that regulate whether certain genes are turned up or down without altering the DNA sequence itself.

## Scientific uncertainty and ethical concerns

The use of DNA testing to assess talents remains controversial. Critics worry that genetic results could be misunderstood or misused, especially when applied to children.

One concern is labeling. If parents are told a child lacks genetic markers associated with a talent, they may discourage the child from pursuing an interest. On the other hand, a child identified as genetically “gifted” may face pressure to perform. Both outcomes could narrow a young person’s choices.

Privacy is another issue. Genetic data is uniquely sensitive: it can reveal information not only about the person tested but also about their relatives. Experts say strict safeguards are needed to prevent misuse by schools, employers, insurers or sports programs.

There is also the risk of commercial exaggeration. Around the world, companies have marketed DNA tests claiming to identify children’s talents in music, math, sports or leadership. Many scientists argue that such claims often go beyond what current evidence can support.

## A fast-moving field with limits

China has invested heavily in genomics, biotechnology and artificial intelligence, and its scientists are increasingly applying large-scale genetic analysis to health, education and performance-related research. As DNA sequencing becomes cheaper, the possibility of using genetic data in everyday decision-making is becoming more realistic.

Still, the scientific consensus remains cautious: DNA can provide useful biological information, but it cannot fully explain complex human abilities such as bravery, persistence or intelligence.

For now, researchers say genetic analysis should be viewed as one tool among many — potentially helpful when combined with observation, psychological assessment, medical evaluation and environmental support.

The message from scientists is nuanced: genes may help shape a person’s starting point, but life experience, training and opportunity help determine how far that person can go.

## In China, Parents Turn to Biotech to Decode Their Children’s Potential — But Science Has Limits

**By [Your Name]**

SHANGHAI — On a Saturday morning in a glass-walled genetics testing center in Shanghai, parents sit with toddlers on their laps while technicians prepare cheek swabs. The children are too young to read, too young to choose an instrument or a sport. But their parents have come hoping biotechnology might offer a clue: Is this child built for basketball? Music? Mathematics? Endurance sports?

Across China’s major cities, a growing number of families are paying for genetic and biometric testing services marketed as tools to help identify children’s “natural strengths.” The services vary widely. Some analyze DNA markers associated with traits such as muscle composition, metabolism or sensory processing. Others combine genetic data with physical measurements, cognitive assessments and family history.

For many parents, the appeal is obvious in a highly competitive society where education and extracurricular training can begin early. If a child has a measurable advantage, parents want to know before investing years — and thousands of yuan — in piano lessons, swimming classes or elite tutoring.

“Parents are not asking us to decide their child’s future,” said Dr. Li Wen, director of a private pediatric biotechnology lab in Shenzhen. “They are asking for information. They want to understand whether their child may be more suited to explosive sports, endurance activities, or certain learning environments.”

But scientists caution that the dream of predicting the next Yao Ming or Yo-Yo Ma from a cheek swab remains far beyond the reach of current biology.

### A Market Built on Hope and Anxiety

China’s interest in child-development testing reflects a broader global trend: the commercialization of personal genomics. Once limited to medical research and disease screening, DNA analysis is now marketed for ancestry, nutrition, fitness and talent identification.

In China, the pressure can feel especially intense. Parents often face fierce competition for places in top schools and extracurricular programs. A child who shows early promise in sports or the arts may gain access to specialized training tracks. That has helped create a market for tests that promise to reduce uncertainty.

At one Beijing lab, parents receive a report that ranks a child’s genetic indicators related to aerobic capacity, muscle recovery, height potential and injury risk. Some packages include recommendations for sports or arts training.

“We tell families this is not a prophecy,” said Chen Rui, laboratory director at a genomics company in Beijing. “It is a probability-based reference. A gene may influence one small part of a trait, but environment, training, nutrition, motivation and opportunity are just as important — often more important.”

Still, the marketing language used by some companies can be bold. Advertisements on parenting forums and social media platforms suggest that testing can help children “avoid the wrong path” or “discover hidden talent early.” Some parents say the reports give them confidence. Others say they leave with more questions than answers.

### The Yao Ming Problem

Height is one of the easiest examples to understand — and one of the clearest illustrations of the limits of prediction.

Yao Ming, the retired Chinese basketball superstar, stood 2.29 meters tall. His parents were both elite basketball players, and genetics almost certainly contributed to his exceptional height. But even height, one of the most heritable human traits, cannot be predicted perfectly in childhood using DNA alone.

Hundreds, possibly thousands, of genetic variants contribute to height, each with a small effect. Nutrition, childhood health and hormonal factors also play roles. A test may estimate a child’s likely adult height range, but it cannot determine whether that child will have Yao’s coordination, discipline, injury resilience, court vision or competitive temperament.

“People think if we can predict height, we can predict basketball success,” said Dr. Zhao Mingjie, director of a sports science laboratory in Guangzhou. “But basketball is not only height. It is balance, timing, coaching, psychology, family support and luck. Yao Ming was not just tall. He became Yao Ming because of a rare combination of body, skill, training and circumstance.”

That complexity applies even more strongly to fields like music. Parents may wonder whether a child has the makings of Yo-Yo Ma, the world-renowned cellist. But musical excellence involves far more than hearing ability or fine motor control. It requires years of deliberate practice, emotional expression, memory, mentorship and personal passion.

“No DNA test can tell you that a child will become Yo-Yo Ma,” said Chen. “At most, science may identify some biological tendencies — perhaps auditory sensitivity or physical traits related to coordination. But artistry is not stored in one gene.”

### What the Tests Can — and Cannot — Say

Many scientists agree that genetic testing can provide useful information in certain contexts. Some tests can identify medical risks, inherited disorders or drug sensitivities. In sports, genetic markers may offer limited insight into traits such as fast-twitch versus slow-twitch muscle tendencies. Biometric assessments can also help identify posture problems, vision issues or injury risks.

But using such information to predict talent is far more uncertain.

Human performance is polygenic, meaning it is shaped by many genes, each contributing a small amount. It is also deeply environmental. A child with a genetic tendency toward strong aerobic capacity may never become a runner if they dislike running, lack coaching or grow up without access to sports facilities. Another child with average genetic indicators may excel through motivation, training and opportunity.

“There is a difference between identifying a potential advantage and predicting a future career,” said Li. “The first is sometimes possible. The second is not.”

Experts also warn that test results can become self-fulfilling or self-limiting. A child labeled “unsuited” for music may never be given the chance to enjoy it. A child labeled “athletically gifted” may face pressure that turns play into obligation.

### Ethical Questions for Families

The rise of child potential testing raises ethical concerns. Children cannot meaningfully consent to genetic testing, yet the results may follow them for years. Data privacy is another concern, especially when sensitive biological information is stored by private companies.

There is also the question of parental expectation. In a culture where success can feel tightly linked to family sacrifice, a report suggesting high potential may intensify pressure on a child.

Some lab directors say responsible companies must be careful in how they present results.

“We refuse to use words like ‘genius’ or ‘future champion,’” said Zhao. “That is not science. Our reports are designed to guide healthy development, not to label children.”

Educators and child psychologists often urge parents to treat testing as one small piece of information, not a roadmap. They argue that curiosity, resilience and enjoyment are often stronger predictors of long-term achievement than early biological indicators.

### Between Science and Aspiration

For parents, the promise of biotechnology is not simply about ambition. Many say they want to avoid wasting time and money on activities that may not suit their children. Others hope testing will reveal strengths that traditional schooling overlooks.

Yet the central tension remains: biotechnology can measure parts of a child’s biology, but it cannot measure destiny.

The next Yao Ming may need height, but also coaching, national sports infrastructure, health and personal drive. The next Yo-Yo Ma may need musical sensitivity, but also years of practice, family support, extraordinary teachers and a love for the instrument that no laboratory can manufacture.

“Potential is not a fixed number hidden in the body,” said Li. “It is something that develops. Biology may open a door, but the child still has to walk through it — and sometimes they choose a different door entirely.”

For China’s anxious and hopeful parents, that may be both the disappointment and the comfort of the new science. A cheek swab might offer clues. It cannot write a life.
